---
title: How astronomers find exoplanets
lang: en
free: true
---

Astronomers detect planets orbiting other stars mostly without ever seeing them directly. The light of a planet is drowned out by its star, so the search relies on indirect signals.

## The transit method

When a planet crosses in front of its star, it blocks a tiny fraction of the light. By watching for these periodic dips in brightness, space telescopes like Kepler and TESS have found thousands of candidate worlds. The depth of the dip hints at the planet's size, and the spacing between dips gives the length of its year.

## Radial velocity

A planet tugs on its star as it orbits, making the star wobble. That wobble shifts the star's spectrum slightly toward blue and then red. Measuring this Doppler shift reveals the planet's mass and orbital period, and was how the first planet around a Sun-like star was discovered.

Combining methods lets astronomers estimate both the size and the mass of a world, and therefore its density — the first clue to whether it is rocky like Earth or gaseous like Neptune.
